questions.question: Q: What is the difference between primary and secondary food processing?

points.text: Primary processing converts raw materials into basic ingredients (e.g. wheat to flour, milk to pasteurised milk). Secondary processing turns those ingredients into finished products (e.g. flour to bread, milk to cheese).

questions.question: Q: Name four types of food additive and their purpose.

points.text: Preservatives (extend shelf life), colourants (improve appearance), flavourings (enhance taste), emulsifiers (allow oil and water to mix), stabilisers (maintain texture), thickeners (add body) (any four).

questions.question: Q: What is food fortification and give two examples.

points.text: Fortification is adding nutrients to food to improve public health. Examples: folic acid in flour, vitamins A and D in margarine, calcium in plant-based milks, iron in breakfast cereals (any two).

E numbers are codes for food additives that have been approved as safe for use within the European Union. They cover preservatives, colourants, flavourings, emulsifiers, and other additive categories.

questions.question: Q: What is genetic modification and why is it controversial?

points.text: GM alters an organism's DNA to produce desired traits (e.g. pest-resistant crops, nutrient-enriched rice). Controversy centres on unknown long-term health effects, environmental impact (cross-pollination with wild species), and ethical concerns about altering nature.

questions.question: Q: Explain how modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) works.

points.text: MAP replaces the air in food packaging with a controlled gas mixture (typically nitrogen and carbon dioxide). This slows bacterial growth and oxidation, extending shelf life without adding chemical preservatives.

questions.question: Q: What is extrusion cooking and what products does it produce?

points.text: A process where food is forced through a shaped opening under high temperature and pressure, cooking and shaping it simultaneously. Used for breakfast cereals, pasta shapes, crisp snacks, and textured vegetable protein.

questions.question: Q: Why are ultra-processed foods a health concern?

points.text: UPFs contain many industrial additives, are typically high in fat, sugar, and salt, and are low in fibre and nutrients. Regular consumption is linked to obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and certain cancers.

markScheme.exemplarAnswer: Primary processing converts raw food materials into basic usable ingredients. Examples include milling wheat into flour, pasteurising raw milk, refining sugar cane into sugar, and slaughtering and butchering animals into cuts of meat. Secondary processing transforms these primary ingredients into more complex finished products: flour into bread, milk into cheese or yoghurt, potatoes into crisps, and cocoa beans into chocolate. Food additives are substances added during processing for specific purposes. Preservatives (e.g. sulphur dioxide in dried fruit) prevent microbial growth and extend shelf life, reducing food waste. Colourants improve visual appeal (e.g. annatto in cheese), flavourings restore taste lost during processing, and emulsifiers (e.g. lecithin) allow oil and water to mix in products like mayonnaise and ice cream. Additives have benefits: they make food safer (preservatives prevent food poisoning), more convenient (longer shelf life), and more appealing. However, there are concerns: some synthetic colourants have been linked to hyperactivity in children, excessive preservatives may cause allergic reactions, and the ease of using additives enables ultra-processed foods high in fat, sugar, and salt. All approved additives (given E numbers in the EU) have been safety-tested, and are used at levels far below harmful doses.
